20|BACKGROUND
21|Darolutamide is a potent androgen-receptor inhibitor that has been associated
22|with increased overall survival among patients with nonmetastatic, castration-
23|resistant prostate cancer. Whether a combination of darolutamide, androgen-
24|deprivation therapy, and docetaxel would increase survival among patients with
25|metastatic, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer is unknown.
26|METHODS
27|In this international, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned patients with meta-
28|static, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer in a 1:1 ratio to receive darolutamide (at
29|a dose of 600 mg [two 300-mg tablets] twice daily) or matching placebo, both in
30|combination with androgen-deprivation therapy and docetaxel. The primary end
31|point was overall survival.
32|RESULTS
33|The primary analysis involved 1306 patients (651 in the darolutamide group and
34|655 in the placebo group); 86.1% of the patients had disease that was metastatic
35|at the time of the initial diagnosis. At the data cutoff date for the primary analysis
36|(October 25, 2021), the risk of death was significantly lower, by 32.5%, in the
37|darolutamide group than in the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.68; 95% confidence
38|interval, 0.57 to 0.80; P<0.001). Darolutamide was also associated with consistent
39|benefits with respect to the secondary end points and prespecified subgroups.
40|Adverse events were similar in the two groups, and the incidences of the most
41|common adverse events (occurring in ≥10% of the patients) were highest during
42|the overlapping docetaxel treatment period in both groups. The frequency of grade
43|3 or 4 adverse events was 66.1% in the darolutamide group and 63.5% in the pla-
44|cebo group; neutropenia was the most common grade 3 or 4 adverse event (in
45|33.7% and 34.2%, respectively).
46|CONCLUSIONS
47|In this trial involving patients with metastatic, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer,
48|overall survival was significantly longer with the combination of darolutamide,
49|androgen-deprivation therapy, and docetaxel than with placebo plus androgen-
50|deprivation therapy and docetaxel, and the addition of darolutamide led to improve-
51|ment in key secondary end points. The frequency of adverse events was similar in
52|the two groups. (Funded by Bayer and Orion Pharma; ARASENS ClinicalTrials.gov
53|number, NCT02799602.)

5|tandard treatment for patients
6|with metastatic, hormone-sensitive pros-
7|tate cancer includes the addition of either
8|docetaxel or an androgen-receptor pathway in-
9|hibitor to androgen-deprivation therapy.1-4 In two
10|randomized, phase 3 trials involving such pa-
11|tients, overall survival was longer among those
12|who received docetaxel plus androgen-depriva-
13|tion therapy than among those who received
14|androgen-deprivation therapy alone.5-8 Subsequent
15|randomized, phase 3 trials have shown that the
16|addition of an androgen-receptor pathway inhibi-
17|tor (abiraterone, enzalutamide, or apalutamide)
18|to androgen-deprivation therapy has greater clini-
19|cal benefit than the use of androgen-deprivation
20|therapy alone.9-12
21|Phase 3 trials of combination therapy with an
22|androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor, androgen-
23|deprivation therapy, and docetaxel have shown
24|conflicting results. In PEACE-1 (A Phase III
25|Study for Patients with Metastatic Hormone-
26|naïve Prostate Cancer), overall survival was longer
27|among patients who received abiraterone in
28|combination with androgen-deprivation therapy
29|and docetaxel than among those who received
30|androgen-deprivation therapy and docetaxel
31|alone.13 In contrast, a subgroup analysis of the
32|ENZAMET (Enzalutamide in First Line Andro-
33|gen Deprivation Therapy for Metastatic Prostate
34|Cancer) trial showed that survival was not longer
35|with enzalutamide, androgen-deprivation ther-
36|apy, and docetaxel than with androgen-depriva-
37|tion therapy and docetaxel alone.12
38|Darolutamide is a structurally distinct andro-
39|gen-receptor inhibitor with low blood-brain bar-
40|rier penetration and limited potential for clini-
41|cally relevant drug-drug interactions.14-17 Studies
42|involving patients with prostate cancer, includ-
43|ing the phase 3 ARAMIS (Androgen Receptor
44|Antagonizing Agent for Metastasis-free Survival)
45|trial involving patients with nonmetastatic, cas-
46|tration-resistant prostate cancer, have shown that
47|darolutamide has potent antitumor efficacy.18-22
48|In the ARAMIS trial, the median metastasis-free
49|survival was almost 2 years longer and the risk
50|of death was 31% lower among patients who
51|received darolutamide with androgen-deprivation
52|therapy than among those who received placebo
53|with androgen-deprivation therapy, and the inci-
54|dence of adverse events was similar in the two
55|groups.21,22 In the phase 3 ARASENS (ODM-201
56|in Addition to Standard ADT and Docetaxel in
57|Metastatic Castration Sensitive Prostate Cancer)
58|trial, we evaluated the efficacy and safety of
59|darolutamide added to androgen-deprivation
60|therapy and docetaxel in patients with meta-
61|static, hormone-sensitive prostate cancer.
62|Methods
63|Trial Design and Conduct
64|This international, randomized, double-blind,
65|placebo-controlled trial was sponsored by Bayer
66|and Orion Pharma. The trial was designed by
67|Bayer and the first and last authors, with sup-
68|port from the protocol steering committee. The
69|institutional review board at each participating
70|institution approved the trial, which was con-
71|ducted in accordance with the principles of the
72|Declaration of Helsinki and the International
73|Council for Harmonisation Good Clinical Prac-
74|tice guidelines. All the patients provided written
75|informed consent.
76|An independent data and safety monitoring
77|board reviewed unblinded safety and efficacy
78|data throughout the trial. The data were col-
79|lected by the investigators, analyzed by statisti-
80|cians who were employed by Bayer, and inter-
81|preted by the authors, including employees of
82|the sponsors. Bayer provided funding for medi-
83|cal writing assistance. All the authors reviewed
84|and approved the manuscript that was submitted
85|for publication. The authors assume responsibil-
86|ity for the completeness and accuracy of the data
87|and for the fidelity of the trial to the protocol
88|and the statistical analysis plan, available with
89|the full text of this article at NEJM.org.
90|Patients and Interventions
91|Patients were eligible for participation if they
92|were 18 years of age or older and had an Eastern
93|Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) perfor-
94|mance-status score of 0 or 1 (scores range from
95|0 to 5, with higher scores indicating greater dis-
96|ability), histologically or cytologically confirmed
97|prostate cancer, and metastases detected on bone
98|scanning, contrast-enhanced computed tomog-
99|raphy (CT), or magnetic resonance imaging
100|(MRI). Eligible patients had to be candidates for
101|androgen-deprivation therapy and docetaxel, in
102|the investigator's judgment. Patients were ex-
103|cluded if they had regional lymph-node involve-
104|ment only (N1, below the aortic bifurcation) or
105|if they had received androgen-deprivation ther-
106|apy more than 12 weeks before randomization,

23|For patients receiving LHRH agonists, the use of

29|Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio
30|to receive either darolutamide (at a dose of 600 mg
31|[two 300-mg tablets] twice daily with food) or
32|matched placebo. Randomization was stratified
33|according to the metastasis stage in the tumor-
34|node-metastasis system (nonregional lymph-node
35|metastases only [M1a], bone metastases with or
36|without lymph-node metastases [M1b], or vis-
37|ceral metastases with or without lymph-node or
38|bone metastases [M1c]) and according to wheth-
39|er the alkaline phosphatase level was below or at
40|or above the upper limit of the normal range.
41|Patients continued to receive darolutamide or
42|placebo until symptomatic disease progression,
43|a change in antineoplastic therapy, unacceptable
44|toxic effects, patient or physician decision, death,
45|or nonadherence.
46|End Points
47|The primary end point was overall survival,
48|which was defined as the time from randomiza-
49|tion until death from any cause. The secondary
50|end points were time to castration-resistant
51|prostate cancer, time to pain progression, symp-
52|tomatic skeletal event-free survival, time to a
53|first symptomatic skeletal event, time to initia-
54|tion of subsequent systemic antineoplastic ther-
55|apy, time to worsening of disease-related physi-
56|cal symptoms, time to initiation of opioid
57|treatment for 7 or more consecutive days, and
58|safety. Definitions of the secondary efficacy
59|end points are provided in the Supplementary
60|Appendix.
61|Assessments
62|During the trial, patients were evaluated every
63|12 weeks for evidence of castration resistance,
64|the initiation of subsequent antineoplastic ther-
65|apy, symptomatic skeletal events, opioid use for
66|7 or more consecutive days, pain progression,
67|the worsening of physical symptoms of disease,
68|and adverse events and serious adverse events
69|that occurred during treatment. Patients under-
70|went contrast-enhanced chest, abdomen, and pel-
71|vic CT or MRI and bone scanning at baseline,
72|within 30 days after the last cycle of docetaxel,
73|and yearly thereafter during trial treatment. Pain
74|was assessed with the use of the Brief Pain In-
75|ventory Short-Form questionnaire, and disease-
76|related physical symptoms were assessed with
77|the use of the Functional Assessment of Cancer
78|Therapy-Prostate (National Comprehensive Can-
79|cer Network) symptom index 17-item question-
80|naire. In safety assessments, adverse events were
81|graded with the use of the National Cancer In-
82|stitute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse
83|Events, version 4.03.
84|Statistical Analysis
85|The sample size was calculated on the basis of
86|the primary end point, overall survival. We esti-
87|mated that approximately 1300 patients would
88|be required to observe approximately 509 deaths,
89|allowing for a 5% dropout rate, which would
90|provide the trial with 90% power to detect a 25%
91|decrease in the risk of death in the darolutamide
92|group versus the placebo group, at a two-sided
93|alpha level of 0.05. The secondary end points
94|were tested with a hierarchical gatekeeping pro-
95|cedure in the order described above only if the
96|primary end point and each preceding secondary
97|end point in the hierarchy were statistically sig-
98|nificant. If the primary end point or a secondary
99|end point did not reach significance, the hierar-
100|chical procedure was stopped, and subsequent
101|analyses were considered to be exploratory.

37|Results
38|Patients
39|Between November 2016 and June 2018, a total
40|of 1306 patients underwent randomization at
41|286 centers in 23 countries. A total of 651 pa-
42|tients were assigned to receive darolutamide and
43|655 patients were assigned to receive placebo,
44|both in combination with androgen-deprivation
45|therapy and docetaxel (Fig. S1 and Table S1 in
46|the Supplementary Appendix). Of these patients,
47|1305 patients (651 in the darolutamide group
48|and 654 in the placebo group) were included in
49|the full analysis set, and 1302 patients (652 in
50|the darolutamide group and 650 in the placebo
51|group) were included in the safety analysis set.
52|Demographic and baseline characteristics
53|were well balanced in the two groups (Tables 1
54|and S2). The median age was 67 years in both
55|groups, most patients (71.1%) had an ECOG
56|performance-status score of 0, and 78.2% of the
57|patients had a Gleason score of 8 or greater
58|(scores range from 6 to 10, with higher scores
59|indicating a more aggressive form of prostate
60|cancer). All the patients had metastatic disease
61|at baseline; 79.5% had bone metastases (metas-
62|tasis stage M1b) and 17.5% had visceral me-
63|tastases (metastasis stage M1c). Most patients
64|(86.1%) had disease that was metastatic at the
65|time of the initial diagnosis.
66|At the data cutoff date for the primary analy-
67|sis (October 25, 2021), the median treatment
68|duration was longer in the darolutamide group
69|(41.0 months) than in the placebo group (16.7
70|months), and a higher percentage of patients in
71|the darolutamide group (45.9% [299 of 651 pa-
72|tients]) than in the placebo group (19.1% [125 of
73|654 patients]) were still receiving the assigned
74|trial treatment. Six cycles of docetaxel were
75|completed in 571 of 652 patients (87.6%) in the
76|darolutamide group and in 556 of 650 patients
77|(85.5%) in the placebo group. The reasons for
78|discontinuation of the trial agent are provided in
79|Figure S1. The median follow-up for overall sur-
80|vival was 43.7 months in the darolutamide group
81|and 42.4 months in the placebo group.
82|Primary End Point
83|The primary analysis of overall survival was per-
84|formed after 533 patients had died (229 patients
85|in the darolutamide group and 304 patients in
86|the placebo group). The risk of death was 32.5%
87|lower in the darolutamide group than in the
88|placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.68; 95% confi-
89|dence interval [CI], 0.57 to 0.80; P<0.001) (Fig. 1).
90|A significant improvement in overall survival was
91|observed despite a high percentage of patients
92|who received subsequent life-prolonging systemic
93|therapies, primarily different androgen-receptor
94|pathway inhibitors, among those who entered
95|follow-up in the placebo group (374 of 495 pa-
96|tients [75.6%]) (Table S3). The overall survival at
97|4 years was 62.7% (95% CI, 58.7 to 66.7) in the
98|darolutamide group and 50.4% (95% CI, 46.3 to
99|54.6) in the placebo group. The treatment effect
100|of darolutamide with respect to overall survival
101|was favorable across most subgroups (Figs. S2
102|and S3).

27|Discussion
28|In this international, randomized, double-blind,
29|placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial involving pa-
30|tients with metastatic, hormone-sensitive pros-
31|tate cancer, overall survival was significantly
32|longer among patients who received darolutamide
33|plus androgen-deprivation therapy and docetaxel
34|than among those who received androgen-depri-
35|vation therapy and docetaxel alone. This survival
36|benefit was observed despite a high percentage
37|of patients who received subsequent life-pro-
38|longing systemic therapy in the placebo group.
39|The survival benefit of darolutamide was consis-
40|tent across most subgroups. The time to the
41|development of castration-resistant disease was
42|significantly longer in the patients who received
43|darolutamide, and improvements were observed
44|with respect to the other key secondary end
45|points. The incidence, severity, and nature of
46|adverse events were consistent with the estab-
47|lished safety profiles of androgen-deprivation
48|therapy and docetaxel.
49|Our results are consistent with those in the
50|PEACE-1 trial, which had a two-by-two factorial
51|design. In that trial, 1173 patients with hormone-
52|sensitive prostate cancer that was metastatic at
53|the time of the initial diagnosis were randomly
54|assigned to receive abiraterone, prostate radio-
55|therapy, neither, or both. All the patients re-
56|ceived standard of care (androgen-deprivation
57|therapy with or without docetaxel). In a planned
58|subgroup analysis involving 710 patients who
59|received docetaxel, overall survival was signifi-
60|cantly longer among those who received abi-
61|raterone than among those who did not (hazard
62|ratio, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59 to 0.96).13
63|All the patients in the ARASENS trial were
64|prospectively assigned to receive androgen-depri-
65|vation therapy and docetaxel. This trial provided
66|clear and compelling evidence that overall sur-
67|vival was significantly longer among patients
68|who received combination therapy with daroluta
69|mide, androgen-deprivation therapy, and docetax-
70|el than among those who received androgen-
71|deprivation therapy and docetaxel alone.
72|Darolutamide was associated with a 32.5% re-
73|duction in the risk of death. The combination
74|did not result in more toxic effects than did the
75|combination of androgen-deprivation therapy and
76|docetaxel alone. In both the phase 3 ARAMIS
77|trial involving patients with nonmetastatic, castra-
78|tion-resistant prostate cancer and the ARASENS
79|trial, there was no more than a 2 percentage-
80|point difference between the darolutamide and
81|placebo groups with respect to the incidence of
82|most adverse events that are commonly associ-
83|ated with androgen-receptor pathway inhibitors.22
84|This trial has several strengths and limita-
85|tions. The large sample size enabled us to con-
86|duct a robust statistical analysis to assess the
87|effect of the addition of darolutamide, an andro-
88|gen-receptor pathway inhibitor, to androgen-
89|deprivation therapy and docetaxel on overall
90|survival and a number of key secondary end
91|points. Most patients who were enrolled in our
92|trial had metastatic disease, with bone metasta-
93|ses, visceral metastases, or both, at the time of
94|the initial diagnosis. Thus, limited information
95|is available on the benefit-risk considerations
96|for patients with metastatic, hormone-sensitive
97|prostate cancer and a better prognosis, includ-
98|ing those with recurrent metastatic disease, node-
99|only metastases, or both. In addition, the effi-
100|cacy and safety of combination therapy are
101|unknown in patients with a poor performance
102|status, because the trial included only patients
103|with an ECOG performance-status score of 0 or 1.

group) were included in the safety analysis set.
